title: Given an array of numbers and a value k, find the kth largest element efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
shortTitle: Find the Kth Largest Element Using a Min-Heap

s1_definition.profdef: The kth largest element is the element that would sit in position k from the top if the array were sorted descending. A min-heap of size k solves it without full sorting: you keep only the k largest elements seen so far in a min-heap, so the smallest of those, at the heap's root, is the kth largest overall. Processing n elements with a size-k heap costs n log k time and k space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants the third-largest transaction of the day from a stream of thousands. A clerk keeps a small tray that holds only the three biggest seen so far, and the tray is arranged so the smallest of those three is right at the front. For each new transaction, if it is bigger than the one at the front of the tray, she throws out the front one and slots the new one in; otherwise she ignores it. At the end, the transaction at the front of the tray is exactly the third-largest, and she never had to sort the whole day's transactions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the k largest in a size-k min-heap, and its root is the kth largest, in n log k time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The kth largest element is the element that would sit in position k from the top if the array were sorted descending. A min-heap of size k solves it without full sorting: you keep only the k largest elements seen so far in a min-heap, so the smallest of those, at the heap's root, is the kth largest overall. Processing n elements with a size-k heap costs n log k time and k space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants the third-largest transaction of the day from a stream of thousands. A clerk keeps a small tray that holds only the three biggest seen so far, and the tray is arranged so the smallest of those three is right at the front. For each new transaction, if it is bigger than the one at the front of the tray, she throws out the front one and slots the new one in; otherwise she ignores it. At the end, the transaction at the front of the tray is exactly the third-largest, and she never had to sort the whole day's transactions.

**One line to remember:** Keep the k largest in a size-k min-heap, and its root is the kth largest, in n log k time.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach sorts the whole array and indexes position n minus k, which is n log n time. That is fine for small inputs but wasteful when k is small relative to n, and impossible when the data is a stream too large to hold. The heap approach is better precisely in those cases.

In Java the heap is `PriorityQueue`, which is a min-heap by default, meaning `peek` returns the smallest element. You iterate the array and `offer` each element. After each offer, if the heap size exceeds k you `poll`, which removes the current smallest. This keeps exactly the k largest elements in the heap at all times. For example `if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();` discards whatever is now too small to be in the top k. After processing everything, `heap.peek()` is the smallest of the k largest, which is the kth largest overall.

Each offer and poll on a heap of size k is logarithmic in k, and you do this n times, so the total is n log k, with only k extra space. That beats full sorting when k is much smaller than n, and crucially it works on a stream because you never need all n elements in memory at once, only the running top k.

A senior-level nuance is the alternative Quickselect algorithm, which finds the kth largest in expected linear time using a partition step like quicksort but recursing into only one side. Quickselect is faster on average, O(n), but its worst case is quadratic and it needs the whole array in memory, so it cannot stream. For money values I use BigDecimal with the heap's natural ordering via compareTo. I choose the heap when data streams or k is small, and mention Quickselect as the expected-linear in-memory alternative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fraud-and-reporting dashboard that must surface the top few largest transactions from a high-volume stream, for example the third-largest transaction, without storing or sorting the entire day's feed. This is exactly the size-k min-heap technique, because it keeps only the running top k.

Problem 2 — Transactions are money amounts, so they must be BigDecimal and compared with compareTo, and the solution must be memory-bounded to k regardless of how many transactions flow through, which the size-k heap guarantees.

In our mini-project we build a `TopTransactions` service that returns the kth largest amount using a PriorityQueue of BigDecimal bounded to size k. The demo feeds several amounts and asks for the third largest, logging each eviction from the heap.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the amounts one thousand two hundred, fifty thousand, three hundred, ninety eight thousand, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, asking for the third largest.

Step 1: Offer one thousand two hundred, heap holds it. Offer fifty thousand, heap holds both. Offer three hundred, heap now holds three elements, which equals k, so no eviction yet. The heap root, the smallest, is three hundred.

Step 2: Offer ninety eight thousand. The heap size becomes four, exceeding k, so we poll the smallest, three hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds one thousand two hundred, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 3: Offer seven thousand five hundred. Size four, poll the smallest, which is one thousand two hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds seven thousand five hundred, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 4: Offer twenty five thousand. Size four, poll the smallest, which is seven thousand five hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds twenty five thousand, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 5: Input is exhausted. The heap holds exactly the three largest amounts, and its root, the smallest of those, is twenty five thousand.

Step 6: We return twenty five thousand as the third largest. We never sorted the full array and never held more than three elements, confirming n log k time and k space.

```
  ═══ LLD — Kth Largest (Min-Heap) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Bounded min-heap (PriorityQueue) — streaming top-k           │
  │  Natural ordering via Comparable (BigDecimal.compareTo)       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TopTransactions only computes kth largest                 │
  │  O: pass a Comparator to rank by a different key              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           TopTransactions             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + kthLargest(amounts[], k): BigDecimal│  O(n log k), O(k) space
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  k ≤ number of amounts
      Post: returns kth largest; heap never exceeds k

  ── State Diagram: Heap size ─────────────────────────────

  [offer] ──size ≤ k──→ keep
  [offer] ──size > k──→ poll smallest (evict)
  [end] ──→ peek = kth largest

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. kthLargest(amounts, k)
  2.   for each amount: heap.offer(amount)
  3.     if heap.size() > k → heap.poll()
  4.   return heap.peek()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The kth largest element is the value that would be in position k from the top if you sorted the array descending. The brute-force way is to sort the whole array and index into it, which costs n log n, but when k is small or the data is a stream, I use a size-k min-heap instead. The idea is to keep only the k largest elements seen so far in the heap, so the smallest of those, sitting at the heap's root, is exactly the kth largest overall.

In Java the heap is a PriorityQueue, which is a min-heap by default so peek returns the smallest element. I offer every element into the heap, and after each offer, if the heap has grown beyond k, I poll once to discard the current smallest, which is now too small to be in the top k. After processing all n elements, the root of the heap is the answer. Each offer and poll is logarithmic in k and I do it n times, so the total is n log k with only k extra space, and it works on a stream because I never hold more than k elements at once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a reporting dashboard that surfaces the top few largest transactions from a high-volume stream, such as the third-largest transaction of the day, without storing or sorting the entire feed. The amounts are money, so they are BigDecimal compared with compareTo, and the memory stays bounded to k no matter how many transactions flow through.

The senior-level point I make is that there is a faster in-memory alternative called Quickselect, which finds the kth largest in expected linear time by partitioning like quicksort and recursing into only one side. I note that Quickselect is faster on average but has a quadratic worst case and needs the whole array in memory, so it cannot stream. That is the trade-off: I reach for the heap when data streams or k is small, and for Quickselect when I have the full array in memory and want expected-linear time.
